Motivation
Kafka clients report latency and size as an average and a maximum over a 30-second window,and nothing elsereaches aMetricsReporter.clients/src/main/javausesnew Avg()36 times,new Max()31 times,andPercentilesnever,so no client latency or size metric has a percentile today.
An average and a maximum are useful,but they don't show how the values are spread out.Say a producer's requestsmostly take 3 to 7 ms,and one request in the window stalls for 2 seconds.The average jumps to about 150 ms,whichno longer looks like a normal request.Neither number tells you that most requests finished under 7 ms,or whetherthe stall was a one-off or the start of a problem.Fetch sizes have the same problem:they stay small while aconsumer keeps up and jump when it reads a backlog,so the average lands between the two but does not represent either scenario (low steady state and peaks during lag).
You can't work out p50 or p99 from an average and a maximum.Kafka'sPercentilesstat can compute them,but noclient metric currently uses it.Using it would mean adding new metrics,which needs a KIP of its own,and it would still giveonly the few percentiles someone picked in advance,each over the same 30-second window:A p99 for the last 30seconds can't be combined into a p99 for the hour.
This KIP adds one stat that counts how many values fell into each range,or bin,and gives those counts to thereporter.The reporter canthen decide which percentiles to compute and over what period, or publish the raw bin counts to a downstream collector.APrometheus reporter can publish the counts as_bucket,_sumand_count,an OpenTelemetry reporter can publishthem as a histogram,and the client's own telemetry(KIP-714)could send a real histogram instead of singlenumbers.
Public InterfacesjavaDistributionSnapshot.javajavaDistributionStat.javajavaDistribution.javajavaGeometricBinScheme.java
Bin 0 is only for zero,which is a common value forrecord-queue-time.That way a metric that only ever recordszero reports zero,rather than a percentile somewhere between 0 and 1.Bin 1 holds everything above zero up tomin.
Every client must compute the bin edges in exactly the same way,because a backend adds up buckets from differentclients only when their edges match exactly.
Changes to existing types
The existing bin schemes,ConstantBinSchemeandLinearBinScheme,include a bin's lower edge and exclude itsupper edge,[low, high).The new scheme does the opposite,(low, high].Thisdefinition aligns withmany metric libraries such asPrometheus and OpenTelemetry.SoHistogram.BinSchemegets a method that says which kind a scheme is.It defaultsto the existing kind (false),so current and third-party schemes keep working.Distributionrefuses a scheme of lower-bounds,so a mistake fails when the metric is registered instead of quietly producing wrong buckets.java
ConstantBinScheme and LinearBinScheme each get a constructor that takes upperInclusive. The existing constructors keep false, so nothing that uses them changes. ratio() uses an upper-inclusive constant bin scheme.ConstantBinScheme, because the precision that matters for a ratio is the same everywhere: 0.30 against 0.35 matters as much as 0.90 against 0.95
KafkaMetricgets a method that tells a reporter whether a metric is a distribution,without reading its value:javaKafkaMetric.java
Sensorgets a method to register a distribution.It is a new method rather than anotheradd,because itbehaves differently:it registers nothing when the client's recording level is lower than the distribution's,forexample aDEBUGdistribution on a client running atINFO,and someone reading the code should be able to seethat.It checks the distribution's own level,not the sensor's,because the sensors these distributions attach toare usuallyINFOeven
